title: S1E3 Celebrity Chef J. Kenji López-Alt
question: In Chinese stir-fry preparation, what mechanisms create the signature tender, velvety meat texture during velveting?
guest: In a marinade, there's a couple things that are going to make the meat more tender. The washing part is really just mechanical breakdown. Physically, it's the same way that pounding meat or using a Jaccard breaks down muscle proteins. Those are going to shorten the muscle proteins, separate them, and loosen them up a little bit so that you just have less work to chew—it's almost like it's been chewed, so that's going to make it more tender. Loosening those fibers is also going to allow them to absorb those marinades more, so you get more flavor. And then the other important part—this is where in velveting you use egg whites, and I generally recommend using a little bit of baking soda also—that alkaline chemistry actually gives the meat an almost slick texture. With Western cooking, often we're looking for that textural contrast between a browned crust and a softer, chewier interior, like a steak or roast chicken. Whereas with stir-fries, we get crunch from other elements—vegetables, nuts, or fried seeds—and the meat is tender, velvety, and slick all the way through. An alkaline marinade is what gives you that texture.

points.core: Vigorous washing mechanically breaks down muscle proteins to reduce chewing resistance.
points.note: Accept: physical massaging, kneading, or squeezing shortening or disrupting muscle fibers like pounding or Jaccard tenderizing. Do not credit: claiming water chemically dissolves proteins or generic 'it softens meat'.

points.core: Loosened muscle fibers absorb marinade liquid more effectively for deeper flavor.
points.note: Accept: separated or relaxed protein structures taking up more marinade or seasoning. Do not credit: generic advice to marinate longer without linking absorption to loosened fibers.

points.core: Alkaline marinade ingredients alter meat proteins to produce a slick, velvety mouthfeel.
points.note: Accept: raising pH with baking soda or egg whites yielding a smooth, slippery, tender exterior throughout rather than a seared crust. Do not credit: acid-based tenderizing or cornstarch alone.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Velveting works through a combination of chemical tenderizing and physical protection.

First, the marinade alters the meat itself. Salt and soy sauce dissolve some muscle proteins (mainly myosin), helping the fibers hold more water. When baking soda is used, it raises the surface pH, pushing proteins away from their isoelectric point so they repel one another, bind more water, and tighten less when heated. Egg white, if included, is also mildly alkaline and adds a soft protein film.

Second, the cornstarch coating forms a barrier. During the brief pre-cook, called "passing through" oil or water at relatively low temperature, the starch gelatinizes into a thin, slippery gel. This layer insulates the meat surface from the wok's fierce heat, slows moisture loss, and keeps the outer proteins from over-coagulating and turning tough. Oil in the marinade keeps pieces separate and adds lubrication.

Third, the gentle blanching sets the coating and partially cooks the meat evenly, so the final stir-fry is very short.

The result is juicy meat inside a silky gel sheath that also grips sauce, which is the "velvet" sensation.

The response discusses water retention but never links loosened fibers to greater marinade uptake or deeper flavor.
The response links alkalinity to water retention and reduced protein tightening while attributing the slippery, velvety mouthfeel to the starch gel.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Velveting (*shàng jiāng*) creates tender, silky stir-fried meat through several complementary physical and chemical mechanisms. Slicing meat thinly against the grain mechanically shortens tough muscle fibers, while massaging in salt and liquid (such as water or Shaoxing wine) solubilizes myofibrillar proteins so muscle cells swell and retain added moisture. Alkaline ingredients—specifically naturally alkaline egg whites or a pinch of baking soda—raise the meat’s surface pH, increasing electrostatic repulsion between protein filaments so they resist contracting tightly and squeezing out juices when heated. Coating the meat with cornstarch, egg white, and a thin film of oil builds a protective barrier: upon heating, the starch gelatinizes and egg proteins set into a smooth, hydrated gel that seals in internal moisture, prevents pieces from sticking, and imparts the signature velvety mouthfeel that helps sauces cling. Finally, briefly par-cooking the coated meat in warm oil (*huá yóu*) or simmering water gently sets this insulating layer before the final high-heat stir-fry, buffering the interior from rapid protein over-coagulation and drying.

points.why: The response credits slicing with shortening fibers and credits massaging with solubilizing proteins, so it misses mechanical fiber disruption during washing or massaging.
The response links protein solubilization to swelling and moisture retention without linking loosened fibers to greater marinade uptake.
The response links alkalinity to reduced protein contraction and juice loss and attributes the slick mouthfeel to the starch-and-egg gel.

noweb.answer: Velveting creates its signature tender, silky texture through protein modification, hydration, and thermal insulation. Slicing meat thinly against the grain shortens muscle fibers, while massaging in salt or soy sauce with water or Shaoxing wine dissolves surface myosin and draws moisture deep into the tissue. Alkaline ingredients like baking soda or naturally alkaline egg whites raise the meat's pH, increasing repulsive negative charges between protein filaments so they retain water rather than contracting tightly and expelling juices when heated. Cornstarch and egg white then coat each slice, with a touch of oil helping pieces separate cleanly. Finally, briefly blanching the coated meat in warm oil or simmering water before stir-frying gelatinizes the starch and sets the egg proteins into a supple, hydrated shell. This delicate barrier buffers the meat from harsh wok heat, prevents surface toughening and moisture loss, and creates a smooth, glossy exterior that helps sauces cling evenly.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Velveting gets its texture from several mechanisms that work together. First, the meat is coated in a marinade of cornstarch, egg white, a little rice wine or water, and often salt. When cooked, the starch gelatinizes and the egg proteins set into a thin, slippery film. This film insulates the meat from direct high heat, slowing moisture loss and stopping the surface proteins from tightening and squeezing out juice.

Second, salt partly dissolves the muscle proteins (myosin) and helps the meat hold water. Many cooks also add a pinch of baking soda. It raises the pH, which pushes the proteins away from their isoelectric point, so they bind more water and contract less when heated. Third, cutting thin slices across the grain shortens the muscle fibers, and the marinade gets in more easily.

Finally, the coated meat is briefly pre-cooked in warm oil (about 120–150°C) or barely simmering water, which sets the coating gently before the meat goes into the hot wok. The result is meat that stays juicy inside and smooth, almost silky, on the surface.

points.why: The response describes shortening fibers by slicing across the grain and omits the mechanical tenderizing action of vigorous washing or massage.
The response attributes easier marinade penetration to thin cross-grain slicing and does not explain how loosened fibers take up more marinade.
The response links higher pH to water retention and reduced protein contraction but attributes the slippery texture to the cooked starch-and-egg coating.
